title: Jeremiah 8:1–13
context: The LORD continues the oracle from chapter 7, announcing that the bones of kings, princes, priests, prophets, and the people of Jerusalem will be brought out of their graves and spread before the sun, moon, and stars they worshiped, unburied (8:1–3). This page reports the image soberly. Jeremiah is then told to bring the LORD’s questions to the people: people who fall rise again, yet Jerusalem clings to deceit and refuses to return; no one asks “What have I done?”; even the stork and the swallow know their seasons, but “my people don’t know the LORD’s law” (8:4–7). The claim “We are wise, and the LORD’s law is with us” is answered with “the false pen of the scribes has made that a lie” (8:8); what this pen wrote or distorted is not specified, and this page does not reconstruct it. Verses 8:10–12 closely repeat 6:12–15, including “Peace, peace,” when there is no peace; this page names the parallel without harmonizing the small differences. Both traditions read the unit as shared ground about refusal to repent and the emptiness of false assurance.

verses.text: “At that time,” says the LORD, “they will bring the bones of the kings of Judah, the bones of his princes, the bones of the priests, the bones of the prophets, and the bones of the inhabitants of Jerusalem, out of their graves.
verses.arminianNotes: The bones of kings, princes, priests, prophets, and people will be brought out of their graves. Arminian readers note that every level of society is included. Those who led and those who followed share in the judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the judgment reaching even the dead, a sign of its completeness. Shared ground: both traditions report the image soberly, without expanding on its details, and see it as continuing the judgment announced in 7:30–34.

verses.text: They will spread them before the sun, the moon, and all the army of the sky, which they have loved, which they have served, after which they have walked, which they have sought, and which they have worshiped. They will not be gathered or be buried. They will be like dung on the surface of the earth.
verses.arminianNotes: The bones will be spread before the sun, moon, and stars they loved and served. Arminian readers note the bitter irony: the heavenly bodies they worshiped cannot help them. They will not be gathered or buried.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the futility of idolatry exposed. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse soberly as showing that the objects of false worship cannot save, and both avoid adding detail to the grim picture the text gives.

verses.text: Death will be chosen rather than life by all the residue that remain of this evil family, that remain in all the places where I have driven them,” says the LORD of Armies.
verses.arminianNotes: “Death will be chosen rather than life by all the residue that remain.” Arminian readers hear the depth of the survivors’ despair. The suffering of exile will be so great that death will seem preferable.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the severity of the judgment on those who remain. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse with pastoral sobriety, recognizing the reality of despair in judgment, and neither expands on it beyond what the text says.

verses.text: “Moreover you shall tell them, ‘The LORD says: “ ‘Do men fall, and not rise up again? Does one turn away, and not return?
verses.arminianNotes: “Do men fall, and not rise up again? Does one turn away, and not return?” Arminian readers note that the LORD appeals to common sense. People who fall get up; people who stray come back. Why will Jerusalem not return?
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the LORD’s pleading question. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as an appeal to ordinary experience that highlights the strangeness of the people’s refusal to repent.

verses.text: Why then have the people of Jerusalem fallen back by a perpetual backsliding? They cling to deceit. They refuse to return.
verses.arminianNotes: Jerusalem has fallen back “by a perpetual backsliding,” clinging to deceit and refusing to return. Arminian readers stress that the refusal is the people’s own choice. They have been called to return and will not.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise affirm the people’s real responsibility and see in persistent backsliding the bondage of a heart set on deceit. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as describing a culpable and continuing refusal to repent.

verses.text: I listened and heard, but they didn’t say what is right. No one repents of his wickedness, saying, “What have I done?” Everyone turns to his course, as a horse that rushes headlong in the battle.
verses.arminianNotes: No one repents, saying, “What have I done?” Everyone rushes on like a horse into battle. Arminian readers note the absence of self-examination. The people never stop to consider their ways but charge ahead in sin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the hardness that refuses to ask the question of repentance. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a sober picture of thoughtless persistence in wrongdoing, and both see self-examination as a mark of true repentance.

verses.text: Yes, the stork in the sky knows her appointed times. The turtledove, the swallow, and the crane observe the time of their coming; but my people don’t know the LORD’s law.
verses.arminianNotes: The stork, turtledove, swallow, and crane know their seasons, “but my people don’t know the LORD’s law.” Arminian readers note the contrast with migrating birds that follow the order God has set. The people fail to do what even birds do.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the created order as a rebuke to human rebellion. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a vivid comparison showing that the people’s ignorance of God’s law is willful and unnatural.

verses.text: “ ‘How do you say, “We are wise, and the LORD’s law is with us”? But, behold, the false pen of the scribes has made that a lie.
verses.arminianNotes: “We are wise, and the LORD’s law is with us,” yet “the false pen of the scribes has made that a lie.” Arminian readers note that possessing the law is no protection when it is mishandled. What the pen wrote is not specified.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a warning against trusting in possession of Scripture while distorting or ignoring it. Both hold the precise meaning loosely. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as exposing false confidence, without reconstructing what the scribes did.

verses.text: The wise men are disappointed. They are dismayed and trapped. Behold, they have rejected the LORD’s word. What kind of wisdom is in them?
verses.arminianNotes: “The wise men are disappointed… they have rejected the LORD’s word.” Arminian readers note that wisdom without God’s word is empty. Those who claimed wisdom are shamed because they set aside what God said.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see that true wisdom begins with receiving God’s word. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as teaching that rejecting the LORD’s word leaves human wisdom hollow, and both apply it to any wisdom that ignores God.

verses.text: Therefore I will give their wives to others and their fields to those who will possess them. For everyone from the least even to the greatest is given to covetousness; from the prophet even to the priest everyone deals falsely.
verses.arminianNotes: Their wives and fields will go to others, for everyone from least to greatest is given to covetousness. Arminian readers note that this verse closely repeats 6:12–13. Corruption reaches prophets and priests alike.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the parallel with 6:12–13 and the universal scope of the charge. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as condemning covetousness and falsehood among leaders and people, and neither harmonizes the small differences in wording.

verses.text: They have healed the hurt of the daughter of my people slightly, saying, “Peace, peace,” when there is no peace.
verses.arminianNotes: They healed the hurt of the people slightly, saying, “Peace, peace,” when there is no peace. Arminian readers note the danger of false comfort. Leaders offered reassurance instead of calling the people to repent (compare 6:14).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a warning against shallow healing that ignores the real wound of sin. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as condemning false assurance from religious leaders, and both note its near repetition of 6:14.

verses.text: Were they ashamed when they had committed abomination? No, they were not at all ashamed. They couldn’t blush. Therefore they will fall among those who fall. In the time of their visitation they will be cast down, says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: “Were they ashamed when they had committed abomination? No.” Arminian readers note the loss of shame as a sign of deep corruption. When people can no longer blush, they have stopped hearing conscience (compare 6:15).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see shamelessness as a mark of hardened hearts, and note the parallel with 6:15. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse soberly as describing a people who will fall because they refused to be ashamed of their sin.

verses.text: “ ‘I will utterly consume them, says the LORD. No grapes will be on the vine, no figs on the fig tree, and the leaf will fade. The things that I have given them will pass away from them.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: “No grapes will be on the vine, no figs on the fig tree.” Arminian readers note the image of a fruitless harvest. The good gifts God gave them will pass away because they did not respond to him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the withdrawal of God’s gifts as part of covenant judgment. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as picturing the loss of blessing, and both see the fruitless vine as an image of a people who did not bear fruit for God.
